newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ dlr crashes over one U.S. cent, hits 19-mth low.
newsitem.headline: NZ dlr crashes over one U.S. cent, hits 19-mth low.

text.p: The New Zealand dollar on Friday morning fell more than one U.S. cent from Thursday's close to under 65 cents, its lowest level since December 1996.
Dealers said the kiwi was being pummelled by hedge funds.
The New Zealand dollar Trade-Weighted Index dropped over 100 basis points to 64.42, its lowest level for 13 months.
"It's heavy, heavy, heavy," said a dealer, saying big selling out of New York had driven the kiwi down.
"The prospects are gloomy. There are no buyers on the horizon whatsoever.
"Unless there is some fundamental change from the Reserve Bank you are going to be looking at 64 cents and you could see it this afternoon. There are just no buyers," he said.
At 10.45 a.m. (2245 GMT) the kiwi was at US$0.6488/95 from its 0.6547/54 open and its 0.6600/07 close on Thursday.
The Trade-Weighted Index was down at 64.60 from 65.60 on Thursday.
The kiwi has now fallen more than nine percent from its high of 0.7150 in mid-November.
"Kiwi is in free-fall, there's no buyers. All the longs are getting out and I wouldn't be surprised if we saw 0.6450 today," another dealer said.
Dealers said the main prospect for a turnaround in the Kiwi was intervention by the Reserve Bank.

The Monetary Conditions Index opened more than 100 basis points below the Reserve Bank's desired level of 825 in the September quarter, but recovered to 66 points below as the 90-day bank bill rate soared 90 basis points to 8.63 percent.
By 10.45 a.m. the MCI stood at 762 -- 63 points below the RB's desired level and 13 points outside the comfort zone.
One dealer said the Reserve Bank was unlikely to comment because bank bill rates had risen so much and the Monetary Conditions Index was still not far outside the RB's 50-point comfort zone.
Meanwhile, dealers said a big U.S. hedge fund was driving the Kiwi lower.

"There's no point standing in his way. He's driving a freight train," a dealer said. "The word is that he's got some money in the bank from other trades this year, he's lost money trying to pick the kiwi top in the past and is keen to have a go this time."
The Australian Financial Review said the kiwi had emerged as a new target for powerful hedge funds.
John Noonan, head of international sales for National Australia Bank in Singapore, said problems facing South East Asian currencies were having a a ripple effect through the region.
"Every currency in the region has been put under the microscope and New Zealand is under a bit of pressure at the moment," he told the AFR.
Some dealers believe the RB's Monetary Conditions Index system is showing flaws.

"The RB two weeks ago said we are going into a period of slowing down, every other normal central bank in a period of slowdown has lower rates, but not these guys, they are cranking them up to eight or nine percent," said a dealer.
He said people are arguing that the RB could make the slump last longer and ultimately the currency and rates will be lower.
"I think they are in a real pickle."
Another dealer said there was a 70-90 percent chance the Reserve Bank would intervene, probably by lowering the cash target to zero or minus.
He expects a rigorous and brief tightening before things were allowed to go back to where they were.
But he said the big rise in bill yields would take some pressure off the RB.
Michael Workman, Forex Strategist with Commonwealth of Australian Bank in Sydney, told Reuters Financial TV that the kiwi was a one-way bet.
"Over the next week or so we believe the downside of the New Zealand dollar will continue to dominate the outlook.
"We are looking for it to go down towards the 64 cent level against the (U.S.) dollar in the very short term," he said.

He said interest rates were adjusting, 90-day bank bills having risen 90 basis points in the morning before adjusting back to 8.45 percent, 75 points higher than at Thursday's close. If the adjustment was sufficient, the Reserve Bank would not
have to intervene, Workman said.
-- Simon Louisson, Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 473-3736
